item.title: Tokenomics 2.0
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Consumption weighted token prices have declined approximately 50% over six months and average token prices have declined 62% at the frontier, reflecting both the growing share of cheaper open-weight models and price cuts by proprietary providers, likely driven by some combination...
item.content:encoded:
Consumption weighted token prices have declined approximately 50% over six months and average token prices have declined 62% at the frontier, reflecting both the growing share of cheaper open-weight models and price cuts by proprietary providers, likely driven by some combination of improved inference efficiency and competitive pressure. Increased competition from open-weight models may exert pressure on margins at the frontier through time, but the expansion of token volume suggests overall inference demand is accelerating.

Open-weight models now account for around 65-70% of smart routing token volume, potentially putting pressure on excess rents at the frontier as cheaper models become “good enough” for a growing range of enterprise tasks, especially given US-developed open-weight models offer greater flexibility around customisation, hosting and data control. Caution is warranted in extrapolating from OpenRouter and Vercel data, since users who self-select into model-routing platforms may be more willing to experiment with and switch between models, exhibiting less inertia than the broader AI customer base; however the direction of travel is nevertheless informative, especially as we expect adoption to become increasingly cost-conscious through time.

The recent stall in total expenditure in Ramp’s monthly spend data provides some further grounds for caution, as it shows essentially no growth in overall enterprise spend in the last two months (Aug and Sept), likely reflecting the interaction of lower token prices with increased volume. The data also implies that 80% of spend on frontier labs is driven by 1% of firms, and that the top 1% spent $9,568 per employee per month in Sept vs the median firm that spent $15.7 per employee per month, illustrating how concentrated spending remains. The recent plateau may prove important as total expenditure determines the revenues available to remunerate the AI investment cycle, and it appears that some combination of lower prices and increased competition from open-source may be causing total spend to flatline. The upcoming October release will be important as more timely token volume data from October imply a further acceleration of inference demand, but the implications for total spend remain unclear given shifts in token prices and composition of spend.

Token volumes have risen approximately 5x over the last 6 months and around 50% over the last four weeks, consistent with a substantial demand response as intelligence becomes cheaper. Where that expansion exceeds improvements in computational efficiency, demand for GPU-hours increases, and GPU rental rates suggest that available compute capacity remains scarce: H100 rentals are up approximately 14% over six months and 7% over the last 30 days, while B200 rentals have risen 27.5% over six months, implying robust demand for compute. Continued strength in older H100s is particularly striking against the depreciation one would ordinarily expect from technological obsolescence, implying sellers of scarce compute are well placed to extract rents.

A firm’s margin on each additional unit of output is the difference between its selling price and marginal cost, so falling output prices and rising input costs squeeze margins unless productivity improves sufficiently to compensate. For the frontier labs, competition from cheaper open-weight models can exert both pressures simultaneously, pushing token prices lower whilst stimulating inference demand that bids up the cost of compute. At unchanged inference efficiency, higher GPU rental rates increase the marginal cost of supplying a token, leaving the frontier receiving less for what it sells whilst paying more to produce it. The question is therefore whether improvements in tokens served per GPU-hour (inference efficiency) can offset both the decline in selling prices and the increase in compute costs in perpetuity. Gross margin can be approximated as follows, assuming compute dominates serving costs and holding workload mix constant:

Using the 27.5% rise in B200 GPU rental rates as an illustrative increase in compute costs, combined with the 50% decline in average token prices requires throughput to increase 2.55-fold, merely to preserve the gross-margin. This is not an unsurmountable issue, as reporting suggests that inference efficiency gains in the last year have been substantial, and compute costs can be locked in via multi year deals. However the marginal economics of inference can still remain a source of pressure, particularly on a forward basis, should open source competition intensify, or should progress on inference efficiency stall. These calculations are illustrative only and intended to highlight the efficiency requirement rather than estimate any individual lab’s margins, since public rental benchmarks differ from contracted compute costs and published token prices differ from realised revenues.

Hence, a clear focus is whether inference efficiency gains can continue to support margins despite intense competition for both market share and compute, particularly as the easier improvements or low-hanging fruit may, through time, become exhausted. New hardware offers greater throughput but also commands higher prices, absorbing some of the incremental benefit. Moreover, as efficiency improves, those same benefits may apply to open-weight models too, such that another round of price cuts may stimulate further inference and renew the pressure on scarce compute, leaving the frontier obliged to deliver further successive gains simply to defend its existing margins. None of this implies that the fundamentals of the business model are broken; however, markets move on gaps between expectations and reality, and we question whether expectations for frontier profitability fully accommodate sustained competition that passes efficiency gains through to customers whilst infrastructure suppliers capture the benefits of scarcity in the form of excess rents.

We consequently see a more nuanced outlook for the AI ecosystem, with strong inference demand favouring suppliers of scarce compute as competition raises questions around excess returns at the frontier. The economics may resemble those of airlines and airports, with frontier labs as the established airlines, providing an essential service to the economy in a highly competitive market and sees open-weight models as the low-cost carriers, expanding the market through cheaper fares whilst constraining what incumbents can charge. The hyperscalers’ infrastructure businesses resemble the airports, with stickier demand and greater scope for higher, more durable margins from supplying scarce compute, and a commercial architecture that is model agnostic in the long run. A reassessment of profitability at the frontier on margin or commoditisation concerns would nevertheless be challenging for the complex as a whole, given how much infrastructure investment rests on future spending commitments. Within that framing, we see the hyperscalers as potentially the most durable beneficiaries of growing inference demand, with diversified cash flows and strong balance sheets allowing them to fund additional capacity and withstand a reassessment of frontier profitability more comfortably than leveraged neoclouds.

item.content:encoded:
Jim Esposito, President of Citadel Securities, opened the Future of Global Markets Conference with remarks on the convergence of technological innovation and geopolitical change. He highlighted the accelerating impact of AI, the growing intersection of technology and national power and the critical role of capital markets in financing the next era of economic transformation.

Key Takeaways

  • Technology and Geopolitics: Rapid technological advancement and geopolitical shifts are reshaping the global order, with computing power, energy and capital increasingly becoming instruments of national power.
  • AI Beyond the Digital World: AI is moving into factories, laboratories, transportation, energy systems and defense, expanding the boundaries of innovation.
  • Capital Fuels Innovation: Like the Industrial Revolution, today’s technological transformation has the potential to create entirely new industries, with capital markets playing a critical role in financing their development.
  • Citadel Securities at Scale: With 1,800+ professionals globally, Citadel Securities executes roughly a quarter of U.S. equity trading volume and processes nearly $800 billion in daily notional trading volume, leveraging its scale to deliver deeper liquidity, sharper pricing and market insights.

item.title: A Conversation with Ken Griffin
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Citadel Securities founder Ken Griffin spoke with Bloomberg’s Dani Burger at our recent Future of Global Markets Conference. Ken and Dani discussed the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, and how investors are becoming more discerning in this rapidly growing mark...
item.content:encoded:
Citadel Securities founder Ken Griffin spoke with Bloomberg’s Dani Burger at our recent Future of Global Markets Conference. Ken and Dani discussed the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, and how investors are becoming more discerning in this rapidly growing market. Read the key takeaways below.

1. Artificial Intelligence: Transformative Potential and the Future of Work

  • The advancement in AI models over just the past year has been absolutely tremendous. In a number of fields, AI is literally game-changing. Work that used to take our PhDs and master’s-level employees four to six weeks can now be completed in a matter of hours.
  • There are three implications:

    –  For workers: AI poses a real threat to certain white-collar jobs. We need to embrace reskilling in a profound way. There’s plenty of talk about it, but very little action.

    –  For corporate America: Competitive moats are being filled in by bulldozers. Companies will need to innovate faster, create more customer value and take costs out faster. That’s ultimately a win for the American consumer.

    –  For entrepreneurs: This is a golden era for new business formation. Startups will unleash products we’ve never even thought of and create opportunities for people who don’t have perfect pedigrees to build successful careers.

  • The history of our free market is that we go through transitions like this. They’re challenging for incumbents and difficult for workers, but ultimately our lives are better.

2. AI Markets: Investors Are Becoming More Discerning

  • For the last several years, investors have largely bought into the AI theme: We’re going to spend hundreds of billions or trillions on data centers and compute. Buy the hyperscalers, buy the chip companies, buy the entire supply chain.
  • Now we’re reaching a point where people are becoming more discerning. Who actually earns the economic rents? Where are the real supply constraints? How long will today’s extraordinary margins persist?
  • GPU overcapacity is a significant risk. GPUs have very low marginal operating costs, much like airlines. When capacity exceeds demand, pricing can go into freefall. We saw a similar dynamic during the telecom buildout in 2000, when excess fiber capacity drove telecommunications prices sharply lower.
  • Investors are also reconsidering the useful life of GPUs. Five- or six-year-old chips may command extraordinary pricing today, but that doesn’t mean those economics will persist for another five or six years. Revenue and valuation assumptions for years seven, eight and nine need to be reconsidered.
  • Corporate America is becoming much more sophisticated about extracting value from AI. Companies are asking where they truly need expensive, state-of-the-art models from OpenAI and Anthropic, and where open-source models can do the job at a fraction of the cost.
  • There is a tension between the enormous spending ambitions of foundational model companies and their customers’ efforts to maximize returns and control costs. The question is whether these models become so indispensable—potentially by solving problems like curing cancer—that customers will pay almost any price.

3. Is AI a Bubble?

  • There are almost certainly bubbles within this moment in time. Radical transformations of our economy are generally intertwined with bubbles.
  • Think about the internet in 1999 and 2000. Some companies had pretty fanciful business models, but the internet fundamentally transformed our lives. I just wish I’d kept my Amazon stock.
  • We’ve seen this with other transformative technologies, including the railroads. What’s left in the wake of these bubbles is often game-changing for the world, and the companies that emerge on the other side can be market leaders for decades.

item.title: Europe’s Choice: Competitiveness, Security, and the Future of the European Union
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Mario Draghi, former Prime Minister of Italy and former President of the European Central Bank, joined Bloomberg Television’s Lisa Abramowicz for a discussion on Europe’s economic outlook, competitiveness and geopolitical challenges. The conversation explored fiscal pressures, mo...
item.content:encoded:
Mario Draghi, former Prime Minister of Italy and former President of the European Central Bank, joined Bloomberg Television’s Lisa Abramowicz for a discussion on Europe’s economic outlook, competitiveness and geopolitical challenges. The conversation explored fiscal pressures, monetary policy, AI adoption, energy security and the reforms needed to strengthen Europe’s position in the global economy.

Key Takeaways

  • Growth and Fiscal Stability: Europe’s sluggish growth and rising fiscal pressures are testing economic stability, with Draghi emphasizing inflation control as the European Central Bank’s priority and a high threshold for intervention in sovereign bond markets.
  • European Competitiveness: Fragmented regulations and incomplete integration of services and capital markets are limiting companies’ ability to scale, underscoring the need for structural reforms to unlock investment and growth.
  • AI and Innovation: Europe’s strongest opportunity lies in accelerating AI adoption across industries such as advanced manufacturing, healthcare and finance, rather than competing directly with the U.S. and China in building computing infrastructure.
  • Energy Independence: Expanding renewables, modernizing electricity grids and mobilizing private capital are essential to reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels and supporting Europe’s transition to a more electrified economy.
  • Security and European Unity: Changing transatlantic relations are pushing Europe to assume greater responsibility for its defense, while Draghi expressed confidence that shared interests will preserve European unity despite political uncertainty.

item.title: Fireside Conversation with Eric Glyman, CEO of Ramp
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Eric Glyman, Co-founder and CEO of Ramp, joined Frank Flight, Head of Macro Strategy at Citadel Securities, for a discussion on how AI is reshaping business operations, productivity and economic growth. Drawing on Ramp’s corporate spending data, Glyman explored the pace of AI ado...
item.content:encoded:
Eric Glyman, Co-founder and CEO of Ramp, joined Frank Flight, Head of Macro Strategy at Citadel Securities, for a discussion on how AI is reshaping business operations, productivity and economic growth. Drawing on Ramp’s corporate spending data, Glyman explored the pace of AI adoption, its implications for the workforce and the evolving economics of artificial intelligence.

Key Takeaways

  • Uneven AI Adoption: While a majority of Ramp’s customers now spend on AI, adoption remains highly concentrated, with the top 1% of businesses accounting for approximately 80% of AI spending.
  • Evolving AI Economics: Declining model costs and intensifying competition are reshaping the AI landscape, potentially shifting value toward application-layer companies that translate intelligence into business outcomes.
  • AI and Business Growth: Ramp’s research found that businesses with higher AI adoption experienced stronger revenue growth, with high-intensity adopters increasing headcount approximately 12% faster than before adoption.
  • Organizational Transformation: AI is prompting companies to rethink traditional workflows and organizational structures, integrating intelligent systems into core functions rather than simply automating individual tasks.
  • Managing AI Investment: As spending on AI becomes a significant corporate expense, businesses will increasingly need tools to manage costs, evaluate returns and optimize their use of AI.

item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Jeff Maurone, Technology COO at Citadel Securities, shared how the firm leverages AI, quantitative research and proprietary technology to deliver actionable market insights and high-quality execution for clients. He highlighted the firm’s technology infrastructure, data-driven an...
item.content:encoded:
Jeff Maurone, Technology COO at Citadel Securities, shared how the firm leverages AI, quantitative research and proprietary technology to deliver actionable market insights and high-quality execution for clients. He highlighted the firm’s technology infrastructure, data-driven analytics and growing collaboration with clients to anticipate market dynamics and solve complex trading challenges.

Key Takeaways

  • AI-Driven Insights: AI and autonomous agents are amplifying human intuition, enabling Citadel Securities to systematically analyze vast amounts of data and answer client questions before they are asked.
  • Predictive Market Analytics: Proprietary tools such as Breakout Probability and Positioning NowCast combine market flows, positioning data and historical trends to provide earlier visibility into shifts in investor holdings.
  • Real-Time Credit Intelligence: The firm’s investment-grade credit heat map provides a customized, real-time view of corporate bond spreads, helping clients track market movements across issuers and sectors.
  • Technology at Scale: Citadel Securities’ research infrastructure supports more than 500 quantitative researchers and over 200 petabytes of data, with 65% of colleagues writing code to develop proprietary trading technology.
  • Client Collaboration: The firm has engaged with more than 100 client technology teams to explore AI adoption, agent development and quantitative research, strengthening partnerships and developing solutions to address client needs.

item.title: The Next Big Bet: Sequoia on the Next Wave of Innovation
item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Alfred Lin and Konstantine Buhler, Partners at Sequoia Capital, joined Nohshad Shah, Head of EMEA Fixed Income Sales at Citadel Securities, for a discussion on the next wave of technological innovation and investment opportunities. The conversation explored Sequoia’s investment p...
item.content:encoded:
Alfred Lin and Konstantine Buhler, Partners at Sequoia Capital, joined Nohshad Shah, Head of EMEA Fixed Income Sales at Citadel Securities, for a discussion on the next wave of technological innovation and investment opportunities. The conversation explored Sequoia’s investment philosophy, the evolving AI landscape, the emergence of autonomous agents and where the greatest opportunities for long-term value creation may lie.

Key Takeaways

  • Investment Discipline: Sequoia prioritizes clarity, conviction, courage, creativity and long-term commitment when evaluating opportunities, emphasizing the importance of backing exceptional founders and challenging traditional investment frameworks.
  • AI Value Creation: While AI infrastructure and foundation models are capturing significant value today, the application layer offers substantial long-term potential as businesses translate AI capabilities into practical solutions.
  • The Agent Economy: Autonomous AI agents are beginning to execute transactions and interact with one another, creating new business models and transforming how consumers and enterprises operate.
  • Computing Demand: The proliferation of AI agents will require significantly greater computing capacity, with growing demand for CPUs, GPUs and new architectures to address emerging infrastructure constraints.
  • Emerging Investment Frontiers: Physical AI, biotechnology and space technology represent potentially underestimated opportunities, particularly as advances in AI accelerate innovation in healthcare, scientific research and other complex challenges.

item.dc:creator: ovaughn
item.description: Henry M. Paulson Jr., former U.S. Treasury Secretary and CEO of Goldman Sachs, joined Jim Esposito, President of Citadel Securities, for a discussion on global economic risks, U.S.-China relations and the implications of AI and energy security. Drawing on his experience navigatin...
item.content:encoded:
Henry M. Paulson Jr., former U.S. Treasury Secretary and CEO of Goldman Sachs, joined Jim Esposito, President of Citadel Securities, for a discussion on global economic risks, U.S.-China relations and the implications of AI and energy security. Drawing on his experience navigating the 2008 financial crisis, Paulson shared lessons on leadership, fiscal discipline and international cooperation in an increasingly uncertain world.
